summary: SVCB DNS records describe how to connect to a named service. This document defines how they describe DNS servers themselves, letting a named DNS server advertise which encrypted transport protocols it supports. Clients can use this to pick an encrypted way to talk to it.

eli5.summary: A phone book entry for a helper can say which secret language the helper speaks. This lets DNS servers list the private ways you can talk to them.

questions: how to advertise doh or dot support in dns
what is svcb for dns servers
how does a dns server advertise doh and dot support
subtitle: How a named DNS server can advertise encrypted transports such as DoT, DoH and DoQ using SVCB records.

tldr.problem: A DNS server named by a hostname has no standard way to tell clients which encrypted transports it supports or where to reach them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SVCB mapping for the dns scheme, with records at _dns names, the alpn and port keys for choosing a transport, and a new dohpath key giving the DoH URI Template.
tldr.outcome: Clients can discover DoT, DoH and DoQ endpoints from DNS, but the mapping is a general baseline, and clients that fall back to insecure DNS when SVCB lookups fail stay open to downgrade attacks.

today: RFC 9461 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2023, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The RFC itself says later specifications are expected to adapt this general baseline for specific configurations.

sections.title: Why DNS Servers Need SVCB
sections.content:
The SVCB resource record type tells clients how to reach alternative endpoints for a service, which may offer improved performance or privacy. A DNS server is often identified only by an IP address, but in some contexts, such as NS records or manual resolver configuration, it has a hostname and sometimes a non-default port.

Each service type that uses SVCB needs a mapping document. This one covers the dns service type, so a DNS server can offer alternative endpoints and transports, including DNS over TLS (DoT, RFC 7858), DNS over HTTPS (DoH, RFC 8484) and DNS over QUIC (DoQ, RFC 9250). It is a general-purpose baseline; later specifications are expected to adapt it, for example for stub-to-recursive resolver communication.
sections.eli5: A DNS server is like a shop. This lets the shop put a sign in the phone book saying which private doors you can use to talk to it.

sections.title: Names and Identities
sections.content:
SVCB record names for DNS services use Port Prefix Naming with the scheme dns. A service at dns1.example.com is queried at _dns.dns1.example.com.

The RFC separates two things. The binding authority is the service name and optional port used as input to Port Prefix Naming. The authentication name is the name used to authenticate the secure transport; it MUST be a DNS hostname or a literal IP address and, unless otherwise specified, is the service name from the binding authority.

For a non-default port, the port goes in an extra prefix. If the binding authority is dns1.example.com:9953, the client queries _9953._dns.dns1.example.com. This lets two DNS services on different ports keep distinct behavior. The default port for unencrypted DNS is 53.
sections.eli5: The record lives at a special address made by putting an underscore name in front of the server's name, and a port number goes in front if it is not the usual one.

sections.title: Parameters: alpn, port and dohpath
sections.content:
The alpn key lists supported protocols. There is no default protocol, so no-default-alpn does not apply. If alpn is absent the client MUST treat the record as incompatible unless some other recognized parameter indicates a supported protocol. If the list includes an HTTP version such as h2 or h3, the record indicates DoH and dohpath MUST be present.

The port key gives the target port. If omitted, clients use the default per transport: 853 for DoT and DoQ, 443 for DoH. The key is automatically mandatory, so a client that does not respect it MUST ignore any record containing it. Because a hostile DNS server could use port to make a client send crafted data to some other TCP service, clients SHOULD NOT support the key unless they trust the server, no elevated implicit access applies, or they restrict the allowed ports to exclude likely confusion targets.

The existing keys mandatory, ipv4hint and ipv6hint apply unchanged.

The new dohpath key is a relative-form URI Template (RFC 6570) encoded in UTF-8. It MUST contain a dns variable and, after DoH template expansion, MUST give a valid :path value. Clients send DoH requests to the HTTPS origin made of the authentication name and the port value, at the expanded path. Clients SHOULD NOT query HTTPS records when using dohpath; the SVCB parameters and address records are used instead, though operators SHOULD publish an equivalent HTTPS record.
sections.eli5: The record says which language to speak, which door number to use if it is not the usual one, and, for web-style conversations, which path to follow once you get there.

sections.title: Examples and Limits
sections.content:
A resolver simple.example that supports DoT on its default port 853 is described by one record with alpn=dot. A DoH-only resolver publishes alpn=h2 with dohpath=/dns-query{?dns}. A larger example lists alpn=dot,doq,h2,h3 with dohpath=/q{?dns}, a second record for DoT on port 8530, and a third for an experimental protocol on another name and port. A name server can also point to a configuration published elsewhere using an AliasMode record with priority 0.

The RFC states some limits. It concerns only the DNS transport and says nothing about whether a service is recursive or authoritative. If the authentication name arrives over an insecure channel such as a glue NS record, the specification cannot stop a client from connecting to an attacker. Implementors need not support every transport. Where resolution speed matters, the TargetName SHOULD follow the usual convention and AliasMode records are NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A server's entry can list one way to talk, or several, each with its own door number. Some entries just say to look in a different phone book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Against an adversary on the query path, clients MUST authenticate the server to its authentication name, which the SVCB contents do not influence. For that reason the RFC does not require DNSSEC.

Downgrade: the attacker cannot impersonate the secure endpoint but can forge a response saying no SVCB records exist. A SVCB-reliant client then only suffers denial of service, but a SVCB-optional client generally falls back to insecure DNS and exposes its traffic.

Redirection: the attacker can alter the transport, port and dohpath to steer queries to any port or path on the same host. The RFC's example is a forged dohpath=/upload{?dns} that makes the client publish every query to a public upload endpoint. Mitigations: clients MUST NOT identify or authenticate themselves in DNS queries except to servers known not to be vulnerable, SHOULD stop querying an endpoint that returns an invalid response, and multiple DNS services MUST NOT share a hostname identifier unless they are similar enough that an attacker choosing between them is harmless.

An adversary on the transport path can only cause denial of service against a SVCB-reliant client, so clients SHOULD switch to SVCB-reliant behavior once SVCB resolution succeeds.
sections.eli5: A trickster can erase the sign in the phone book or point it at the wrong door of the right shop. The client keeps checking it really is talking to the right shop, and never hands over its own ID.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added a new entry to the Service Parameter Keys registry: number 7, name dohpath, meaning DNS-over-HTTPS path template, with the IETF as change controller. IANA also added the SVCB node name _dns to the registry of underscored and globally scoped DNS node names.

An appendix summarizes the mapping: scheme dns, RR type SVCB (64), name prefix _dns for port 53 or _$PORT._dns otherwise, and port as the only automatically mandatory key.
sections.eli5: The official list of allowed record fields got one new entry so that everyone agrees what the new field means.
